newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba faces no new need to cut rates - economists.
newsitem.headline: Buba faces no new need to cut rates - economists.

text.p: Germany faces no pressing need to adjust its interest rates and the Bundesbank is likely to keep its three main rates steady this week, pushing out the timing of an easing that many economists still expect in 1997.

In a Reuters poll, 10 economists unanimously forecast the central bank's policy-making council would vote to keep the discount and Lombard rates at 2.50 and 4.50 percent respectively at Thursday's regular scheduled meeting.
They also predicted Germany's main money market rate, the repo, would again be fixed at three percent, the rate which has prevailed since late August.

"There is no reason for a change," said Steven King, economist at James Capel in London, echoing a common sentiment that nothing had changed since the German central bank left rates steady two weeks ago.

Not even much weaker than expected December manufacturing orders, which fell 1.4 percent, were seen as enough to convince the central bank that another rate cut was either necessary or even capable of breathing new life into the economy.

Stressing that such data was often revised significantly, Klaus Holschuh, head of bonds research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt, said neither Wednesday's weak orders data nor Tuesday's strong output data "signalled a change in the trend".
Economists stuck to the argument that rates would remain steady because the mark's levels did not allow an easing and a rate cut would be ineffective.
"The economy has enough liquidity," said WestLB economist Thomas Kull, adding "if the economy does not pick up, then it is not the Bundesbank's fault."
Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said at the World Economic Forum in Davos at the weekend that the council saw no need to cut rates now.
As Gaddum does not speak very ofen and is considered to be well informed, economists give his remarks particular weight.
In fact some argued an interest rate hike was now becoming a much more likely scenario than another cut.

Sharda Persaud, economist at Sao Paolo Bank in London, said: "A lot of strength is coming into the German economy, especially in production and consumption due to the impetus of the export side. If inflation rises to above 2.5 percent, an increase in interest rates is rather likely to happen than another interest rate cut."

But other economists still expect to see a further repo rate cut this year, even if is interpreted merely as a symbolic gesture. Conditions may already be right for some sort of larger repo rate when currency rates normalise.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer last week said he expected the normalisation of the mark's exchange rate against the dollar to end soon, leaving the dollar near 1.64 marks.
"If the dollar slips and the mark rises, there could be some cut in the repo rate," said Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber in London.
For SBC Warburg economist Armin Kayser the psychological importance of another possible rate cut weighed heavily on his forecast that another easing was still likely.
"There is still chance for rate cuts even as Bundesbank officials make stark comments to the contrary. A rate cut would send a psychological signal to the economy," he said.
